front.title: Directwire Agent Fast Transport: A Message-Oriented UDP Transport for MCP/A2A Agent Messaging

abstract.t: This document specifies a message-oriented transport for agent messaging, designed as a QUIC-style fast channel for protocols such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A). Messages are the unit of delivery: a short message (within an unscheduled window) is delivered in a single packet round trip without any grant handshake, while long messages are paced by receiver-driven GRANT scheduling approximating Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT). An eight-level priority queue keeps short interactive requests from being blocked behind bulk transfers, and receiver-driven RESEND/GRANT provides loss resilience. The transport is implemented as stateless cores with no I/O coupling and no runtime randomness, so behavior and performance are deterministic and reproducible.

This document is an informational draft describing the protocol as implemented by the reference implementation agent-transport (Rust). It is intentionally transport-framing-only: application semantics such as tool-call routing and authentication are outside its scope.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Today's agent messaging — Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A) — runs on HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket: byte-stream framing plus per-message header overhead and head-of-line blocking. When a large artifact transfer shares a connection with short interactive requests, the short requests queue behind the bulk transfer. This document specifies a transport that treats messages, not bytes, as the unit of delivery, and in which the receiver — not the sender — drives scheduling. It is designed for the request pattern that dominates agent workloads: many small round trips with occasional large transfers (context snapshots, tool outputs, media artifacts).

The design is a Homa-style receiver-driven approach realized on plain UDP datagrams, without data-center network-priority machinery: eight sender-side priority classes carry the QoS, and the receiver grants transmission credits per message. The transport has four design goals:

li.t: Single-packet round trips. A message no larger than the unscheduled window is delivered in one round trip; no setup, no handshake, no frame parsing.
Short traffic is never starved. Receiver-driven SRPT scheduling and sender-side priority queues keep interactive requests ahead of bulk transfers.
Loss resilience. Receiver-driven RESEND requests and GRANT retransmission repair loss without sender-side congestion control stalls.
Determinism. The core is pure state machines with no I/O coupling and no randomness, so tests and benchmarks are bit-reproducible.

section.t: Current IETF agent-transport efforts build on Media Over QUIC (MOQ) and are sender-driven ; the receiver-driven scheduling specified here is the complementary design point, and the reference implementation's benchmark provides a head-to-head comparison basis.
The wire format is specified in Section 3. The reference implementation and a reproducible benchmark are published at .

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: The unit of application delivery: an ordered byte sequence identified by a sender-assigned 64-bit message ID.
A fixed-size fragment of a message carried in one DATA packet.
A receiver-issued cumulative permission to send bytes up to a given offset.
The leading bytes of a message that are sent without waiting for a grant.
Delay of one message behind unrelated bytes of another message sharing the same byte stream.

section.name: Transport Model
section.t: The transport carries UDP datagrams between two endpoints over a single socket. A message is split into chunks of at most packet size bytes (22-byte header plus payload). A short message fits in the unscheduled window and its first chunk is sent immediately; the receiver delivers the message as soon as all chunks arrive, without any grant exchange. A longer message sends only its unscheduled window initially; subsequent chunks are transmitted only after the receiver grants the corresponding cumulative offset.

Any number of messages may be in flight concurrently over one socket, multiplexed by message ID. The transport is at-least-once: an RPC layer re-sends an entire request (same message ID) on timeout, and receivers deduplicate completed message IDs. Application handlers MUST therefore be idempotent, or perform exactly-once enforcement at the application layer based on message ID.

section.name: Packet Format
section.t: Every packet is a UDP datagram whose first 22 bytes are a fixed little-endian header (no alignment padding), optionally followed by a payload for DATA packets.
For DATA packets the payload length MUST equal the Length field; a receiver MUST discard a datagram whose payload length mismatches. A receiver MUST discard a packet whose Type is unknown.

dl.dd: Carries the message chunk in [Offset, Offset+Length). Message Length is the total message size. The receiver writes the chunk into a reassembly bitmap and delivers the message when the bitmap is complete.
Receiver-to-sender: grants transmission of bytes up to Offset (cumulative). Length is the newly granted span. The sender transmits any chunks in the newly unlocked range.
Receiver-to-sender: requests retransmission of [Offset, Offset+Length), covering all missing chunks in the granted window in one request (batch repair of burst loss).
Receiver-to-sender: concurrency limit reached; the sender SHOULD pause and probe again later. No payload fields are used.

section.name: Priority
section.t: The sender classifies DATA packets into one of eight priority queues derived from the message length. Control packets (GRANT, RESEND, BUSY) are small and influence scheduling liveness, so they are sent directly without queueing.
The queue drains highest priority first (FIFO within a class), so a burst of low-priority chunks from a long message does not block a short, high-priority request.

section.name: Receiver-Driven Scheduling
section.t: The receiver drives transmission credits. The sender may send the unscheduled window immediately; beyond it, chunks wait for a GRANT.

Periodically, the receiver recomputes its grant set. It ranks incomplete messages by remaining bytes (Shortest Remaining Processing Time) and grants the first K (the overcommit parameter, default 2), approximating Homa's over-commitment so that a single grant does not starve other messages. A newly arriving short message preempts a longer message's grant cadence; because grants are cumulative, the displaced message retains its already-granted quota. Messages waiting longer than a starvation threshold MUST be admitted to the grant set, guaranteeing progress.

Loss recovery is also receiver-driven. A chunk missing from the granted window for longer than the resend timeout triggers one RESEND covering the whole missing span. If a grant produces no progress within the grant timeout, the receiver re-issues the GRANT (the original may have been lost). If a sender is idle past the poke timeout, it re-sends its last chunk as a probe, prompting the receiver to issue RESEND or GRANT.

After a sender transmits the final chunk it retains the message state for a short linger period so that a late RESEND for the tail can still be answered; without this, the peer could wait forever for a packet the sender already discarded.

section.name: Reliability
section.t: Delivery semantics are at-least-once. The RPC layer assigns a message ID once and re-sends the entire request on timeout with the same ID. The receiver keeps a bounded cache of recently delivered message IDs and drops duplicate DATA for them, and while a request is being computed it drops duplicate requests for the same ID, so an application handler runs at most once per message ID. Applications requiring exactly-once effects MUST deduplicate or drive state machines on message ID themselves.
A message whose resends go unanswered beyond a bound (default 40) is considered abandoned; the receiver removes it from the grant set so a dead sender cannot wedge the scheduler.

section.name: Determinism and Reproducibility
section.t: The sender and receiver cores are pure state machines: they take packets and a clock as input and produce actions as output, with no I/O coupling and no runtime randomness. Tests exercise scheduling, reassembly, and retransmission as deterministic state-machine transitions. The reference implementation ships a fixed-workload benchmark (fixed operation count, fixed payload sizes, zero randomness) whose workload constants are protected by a fingerprint, so any machine re-running the published baseline produces the same workload and comparable numbers. This is what makes performance claims auditable rather than asserted.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document defines a transport framing; it does not provide authentication, confidentiality, or integrity. Operators MUST deploy it over a secured channel or a securing layer: DTLS for datagrams, or an application-layer authentication and authorization envelope (as used by the MCP and A2A application layers).

The transport is vulnerable to spoofing of GRANT, RESEND, and DATA packets from an on-path or off-path attacker who knows the socket pair. A GRANT inflates the sender's transmission window; a RESEND causes retransmission. These effects are bounded (a grant never exceeds message length; a resend only retransmits already-owned data), but the transport does not resist traffic amplification or message forgery. Receivers SHOULD rate-limit per-source packet processing and SHOULD validate the origin before acting on control packets.
